item.title: Ninety years on, the great Long March spirit is a light shining on the world: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23 00:36:00
Marching toward prosperity. Illustration: Liu Rui/GT The great Long March spirit has been deeply etched into the DNA of Chinese society. It is the determination to rise to challenges and to persist for the long haul; it is the courage to fear no sacrifice and to dare to try; it is the clarity to face reality and actively seek change; and above all, it is the original aspiration of standing with the people through life and death, sharing weal and woe, and striving arduously. The 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March of the Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Red Army was commemorated at a grand gathering in Beijing on Thursday morning. General Secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee Xi Jinping, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, attended the gathering and delivered an important speech. Xi stressed that the great spirit of the Long March demonstrates the power of loyalty, truth, justice and unity. As an important part of the spiritual lineage of the CPC, it transcends time and space and remains evergreen. It will always be a precious treasure and a powerful driving force inspiring us to overcome difficulties and forge ahead courageously. The Long March was a beam of light that burst forth from the Chinese nation at its darkest hour. It showed the world clearly that, even in an old China mired in darkness with no visible way out, there was a group of people striving with all their might to build a new China. In the book The Life Millennium: The 100 Most Important Events and People of the Past 1000 Years, published by the American Time-Life Books, scholars from around the world jointly selected 100 events that shaped the world from 1000 to 2000 AD. The Long March of the Red Army was one of three historical events from China to make the list. It profoundly inspires people that as long as one remains firm in will and unyielding in the face of setbacks, a way out can always be found through continuous exploration, and an entirely new path can be opened. From Edgar Snow to Henry Kissinger, from Nelson Mandela to Fidel Castro, many observers and strategists have pondered why this Long March in the East was able to succeed. To this day, whenever China astonishes the world with technological breakthroughs or reshapes perceptions with development miracles, the world still asks: "How do the Chinese do it?" These questions all point to the same answer: We have found the right path - a path of never yielding, always moving forward, and never retreating. The Long March is both a spiritual treasure that inspires the Chinese people and a display of the Chinese nation's resilient character to the world. Today, the term "Long March" has become a shared name for any arduous journey that ultimately reaches its destination. In this sense, the value of the Long March lies not only in the arrival itself, but in the act of continuing to set forth, again and again. After the victory of the Long March, the nation did not stop: It kept marching through the flames of the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, kept advancing on the tide of reform and opening-up, and continues to advance under the call of the new era, all the way toward the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Today, the great Long March spirit has been deeply etched into the DNA of Chinese society. It is the determination to rise to challenges and to persist for the long haul; it is the courage to fear no sacrifice and to dare to try; it is the clarity to face reality and actively seek change; and above all, it is the original aspiration of standing with the people through life and death, sharing weal and woe, and striving arduously. Ninety years on, the great Long March spirit no longer belongs only to history; it is a light that grows ever brighter and shines upon the world. Currently, global governance is experiencing a "darkest hour": climate change, the North-South divide, geopolitical conflicts, and the undercurrents of deglobalization. Old paradigms are failing, and new rules have yet to take shape. Solving many major issues requires long-term planning and sustained effort that transcend political cycles and short-term gains and losses. The spirit of firm conviction, unity and cooperation, and unyielding struggle transcends national borders and ideologies. It inspires humanity to overcome adversity and pursue a brighter future. This both suggests that global governance needs to blaze new trails toward common development, common security, and common prosperity, and helps the world better understand the spiritual bedrock of the Chinese nation, enabling outsiders to better grasp where this "enabling great power" is heading. "Where the spirit lies, there lies the strength." The great Long March spirit resonates with the Chinese nation's cultural tradition of constant self-improvement and has gained new contemporary meaning in the process of Chinese modernization. While it is no longer possible for China today to replicate the march back then, this spirit will always remain, proving to the world that the Chinese nation possesses extraordinary resilience. After decades of struggle, China has long since become the world's second-largest economy and is comprehensively advancing the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. The enduring national resilience behind the great Long March spirit has been a key factor in creating this development miracle. It is the confidence that allows China to navigate storms and seize the historical initiative, and it also provides a stabilizing expectation for a world full of uncertainty. In the 1980s, Zbigniew Brzezinski, who once served as US national security advisor, walked with his family along the route once taken by the Red Army. He later reflected: "The Long March is more than an epic of almost unmatched heroism." Today, more and more foreigners are coming to China to retrace the Long March route, and places like Loushan Pass have once again become a popular destination for visitors. This is one indication that the great Long March spirit is increasingly needed by the world. As a spiritual monument that the Chinese nation has offered to the world, its importance will become even more prominent in the future. As military writer Wang Shuzeng once described: "The Long March belongs to that category of events in human history which, even after the passage of long years, continue to be sought after by people." "The history of the Long March has never faded; the road of the Long March continues to extend." For China, on the new journey, the Long March has no endpoint. To carry forward the great Long March spirit is to always maintain a high-spirited posture of storming passes and seizing fortresses, to continue the arduous trek on the journey of Chinese modernization, and to respond to all risks and challenges with an unstoppable fighting spirit. It is to both successfully navigate the Long March of our own generation and infuse a world marked by turbulence and transformation with confidence and strength from the East.

item.title: Xi calls for new achievements on new Long March
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 23:54:00
A gathering commemorating the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March is held at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, on October 22, 2026. Photo: CNS Photo Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday called for new achievements on the new Long March as China commemorates the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March. "Only by remembering history can we create a brighter future," said Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, when addressing a gathering held in Beijing to mark the anniversary, according to the Xinhua News Agency. The Long March was an epic military trek from 1934 to 1936 that broke through the encirclement of Kuomintang forces. Some Red Army soldiers marched as far as 12,500 kilometers, in a maneuver that helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution. Nine decades later, the anniversary offers an opportunity to consider how the lessons of that journey continue to inform China's development. Chinese experts pointed to self-reliance, decisions grounded in reality and the ability to adapt under pressure as sources of strength for the country's modernization, from scientific innovation and the green transition to military development. Long March spirit "This earth-shattering revolutionary feat holds great significance in the history of our Party, country and military, and has a profound impact on our path toward the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation," Xi noted, according to Xinhua. He said the great spirit of the Long March demonstrates the power of loyalty, truth, justice and unity. "It will always be a precious treasure and a powerful driving force inspiring us to overcome difficulties and forge ahead courageously." That spirit emerged from a struggle for survival. In 1934, the CPC was forced to abandon its main base in Jiangxi and Fujian provinces after failing to repel the Kuomintang regime's fifth encirclement and suppression campaign. That October, some 86,000 Red Army soldiers crossed the Yudu River in East China's Jiangxi Province and embarked on the grueling 12,500-kilometer journey. Many lost their lives during the roughly two years that followed. American journalist Edgar Snow hailed the journey as "an odyssey unequaled in modern times." Revisiting this history is about drawing wisdom and strength for further progress, Yang Zhe, an associate professor at the School of Marxism at Beijing Forestry University, told the Global Times. Looking back after 90 years offers a deeper understanding of why the victory was inevitable and of the principles that enabled the CPC and the people's military to advance, Yang said. The significance of the anniversary therefore extends beyond remembering a military expedition. It also invites reflection on the path China has traveled and the choices that will shape its future. Seeking truth from facts was a crucial element of the Long March spirit, Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times. The victory depended on strategies, tactics and strategic guidance grounded in actual conditions, together with the Party's absolute leadership over the military, he said. These principles helped establish the correct course for the Red Army, Song said. The experience demonstrated the importance of combining firm leadership with an accurate understanding of the circumstances in which decisions must be made. New journey During the address, Xi said the road of the Long March continues to extend. "On our new journey, we are now committed to realizing the Second Centenary Goal of building China into a great modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on all fronts through a Chinese path to modernization," he said, Xinhua reported. To forge ahead on the new Long March, Xi said, it is imperative to stay committed to the Party's ideals, convictions and purpose and rely closely on the people to create new achievements. The Long March was a turning point in CPC history, and its significance lies in both the victory and the experience and lessons it left behind, Yang said. Those lessons remain relevant when established approaches failed to provide adequate answers to new problems. "When faced with difficulties and setbacks, we must find a way forward based on our own circumstances, rather than mechanically applying established doctrines or simply copying others' experience," Yang added. Navigating an increasingly complex and unpredictable international environment requires strategic resolve alongside tactical flexibility, Yang said. "Today, as China advances modernization amid profound global changes, we face new 'snow-capped mountains' and 'grasslands.' The way forward must be forged through action and exploration." Chinese observers noted that profound global changes are accelerating and reshaping international cooperation and competition. China's development faces strategic opportunities alongside risks and challenges. While opportunities outweigh challenges, uncertainties are increasing. Against that backdrop, China is playing a growing role as a stabilizing force internationally while advancing in fields including nature, technology and energy. An October 14 news feature in Nature described China as one of the world's largest spenders on research and development, a leader in patent applications and a dominant force in research into dozens of crucial technologies, including nuclear energy and synthetic biology. Chinese universities and research institutes are rivaling established Western academic leaders and have reached the top of the Nature Index rankings for the first time, the feature said. Beyond spending and rankings, the report highlighted breakthroughs attracting global attention, from the development of game-changing artificial intelligence models to the first successful retrieval of rock samples from the far side of the Moon. "Instead of competing mainly through its advantages in low labour costs, China is increasingly competing through its technological abilities, innovation ecosystems and the control of technologies," Hao Bin, an economist at Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University in Suzhou, was quoted by Nature as saying. China's green transition offers another example of its changing development capabilities. In the first half of 2026, China's installed renewable energy capacity reached 2.455 billion kilowatts, accounting for 60.7 percent of its total power generation capacity. By the end of July, solar photovoltaic power had overtaken coal to become the country's largest power source by installed capacity. These advances take place amid geopolitical conflicts and overlapping crises. The ability to identify shortcomings and make timely adjustments is essential to opening new possibilities under difficult conditions, Yang said, describing it as a lesson from the Long March that remains relevant to challenges in semiconductors, technological self-reliance and the green transition. Rigorous Party self-governance The drive for modernization also extends to national defense. Xi emphasized the importance of moving more quickly to reinforce the people's armed forces to world-class standards and adhering to the Party's absolute leadership over the military. It is also vital to uphold the leadership of the Party, strengthen Party building and persevere with full and rigorous Party self-governance, he added. An August 1 PLA Daily article marking Army Day described the effort to build a strong military as a cause requiring sustained work across generations. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), the military should build on achieving its centenary goals and press ahead toward basically realizing the modernization of national defense and the armed forces, the article said. This places new and higher demands on pursuing that modernization with high quality. For Song, the Party's leadership over the military, equipment development and the course of military modernization are all part of the new Long March. The Red Army once faced severe limitations in equipment; today, China's stronger economy and technological capabilities provide a foundation for further advances in its defense industry and modern weaponry, he said. An increasingly complex international environment and the need for stronger combat and equipment capabilities make the lessons of the Red Army's victory particularly relevant, Song said. "China's military modernization is itself a new Long March. Remembering the experience behind the Red Army's victory will help the PLA achieve even greater successes."

item.title: China's NDRC issues updated outbound investment rules as overseas investment stock tops $3.4 trillion
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 23:22:00
Domestically produced vehicles are ready for export overseas at the Taicang port zone of Suzhou Port, East China's Jiangsu Province on July 14, 2026. Photo: CNS Photo The National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), China's top economic planning agency, has announced revised administrative measures for outbound investment, aiming to provide stronger institutional safeguards for its development and security. Government officials and analysts said that the updated rules, which include articles asking companies to make annual reports on sensitive overseas investment, will better protect the rights and interests of companies making outbound investment and help investors guard against risks as China's overseas investment expands in a more volatile global market. The rules support investors conducting outbound investment according to market principles and participating in international cooperation and competition. Investors have the right to make their own investment decisions, bear their own risks, and assume responsibility for their own profits and losses, according to a notice posted on the NDRC's website on Thursday. The new rules requested pre-investment approval by the NDRC for projects in sensitive countries and regions such as those in conflict and sectors such as weapon development and cross-border water resource development. Non-sensitive investment exceeding $300 million needs to go through a file and documentation process. Along with high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, China's outbound investment has achieved substantial development, with flows rising from $158.3 billion in 2017 to $213.6 billion in 2025, and the overall investment stock increasing from $1.8 trillion to $3.4 trillion. Outbound investment has steadily promoted the "going global" of Chinese products, services, brands, and standards, enabling domestic investors to obtain investment returns and creating many job opportunities, an NDRC official said in a statement posted on the agency's website on Thursday. However, the external environment has undergone complex and profound changes, with rising unilateralism and protectionism and frequent local conflicts and turbulence, increasing the risks of outbound investment, the NDRC official said, explaining the necessity of the new measures. In addition, a small number of countries and regions have in recent years adopted discriminatory measures, with some requiring the Chinese side to provide technology or data or to dispose of equity or assets, harming China's rights and interests. In response to such issues, the new measures implement the provisions on outbound investment protection under the State Council's regulations on outbound investment, improve the reporting system for major adverse situations, and establish an annual reporting system for outbound investment information, the NDRC official said, noting that investors reporting such situations to the administrative authorities will help pool efforts to protect outbound investment rights and interests. The new rule will take effect on December 1, superseding the incumbent rule imposed in 2017. Song Wei, a professor at the School of International Relations and Diplomacy at Beijing Foreign Studies University, told the Global Times on Thursday that the new measure will further Chinese companies' "going global" drive by setting up more safeguard mechanisms to cope with rising risks in overseas markets amid protectionist headwinds, rising unilateralism and geopolitical conflicts. "The enhanced protection and service by government departments as well as the improved reporting system will enhance companies' ability to avert and overcome risks and market failure, encouraging outbound investment to grow in both scale and quality," the expert said. At a press conference held by the State Council Information Office on Thursday, an official with China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) noted that that during the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-25) period, China's two-way investment remained among the world's leaders. Cumulative utilized foreign direct investment over the five years exceeded $750 billion, and non-financial outbound direct investment covered nearly 190 countries and regions, with cumulative investment exceeding $800 billion over the five years, according to Vice Commerce Minister Jiang Chenghua. China's outbound investment stock ranked among the world's top three for nine consecutive years as of the end of 2025. In the first three quarters of this year, outbound direct investment reached $128.62 billion, achieving steady and orderly development, according to the MOFCOM. Analysts said that as China's outbound investment continues to expand in scale and improve in structure, many emerging markets stand to benefit. "China's robust growth in manufacturing upgrading offers a wide range of opportunities for developing countries in terms of overseas investment and international supply chain cooperation," Wichai Kinchong Choi, a senior expert at Thailand's Kasikorn Bank, told the Global Times on Thursday. In recent years, China's investment in Thailand has become increasingly technology-intensive, covering fields such as electronic components, circuit boards, smart home appliances, data centers, and electric vehicles. These investments are highly consistent with Thailand's industrial development direction and are areas the Thai government intends to develop, playing a positive role in promoting Thailand's industrial upgrading, Choi said.

item.title: GT Voice：What does Japan get in return for investing in US chip plants?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 22:19:00
An AI-generated image of a chip Photo: VCG While Japan is in the midst of a major push to revive its chip sector, it is being pressed to build America's, Reuters reported on Tuesday. The report comes after news that Japan will invest up to $21 billion to build two chip factories in New York state that will be jointly owned by the US government and Japanese interests and operated by GlobalFoundries. It is part of a pledge to invest $550 billion in the US made with the Trump administration in return for lower tariffs. While the investment appears to be a deepening of the US-Japan alliance, it is actually a costly drain on Japan's reboot of its semiconductor sector. Some may believe that investment in the US and domestic investment can be compatible, and they will both benefit Japanese equipment manufacturers. But the bilateral agreement reached in 2025 already showed that the US is the side that could benefit significantly from Japan's investment. Japan's investment projects will be selected and managed by the US, and cash flows generated by the investments are to be split equally until Japan recoups its "deemed allocation amount," after which 90 percent of the cash flow will go to the US. This arrangement means Japan is putting up its capital to build up America's domestic chip production capacity, only to end up with meager returns. Some have already pointed out that this kind of investment is essentially a "tax" in exchange for lower tariffs for Japanese exports to the US. This is the core reality that should not be overlooked: in Washington's calculation, the industrial capabilities of its allies are resources to be mobilized and made to bear the costs of America's own industrial priorities. The so-called "Chip Alliance" - publicly framed as a collective effort to safeguard global supply chain security - is in essence a mechanism that pulls the fiscal resources of US allies directly into Washington's industrial policy toolbox. The allies pay the bills, the US builds the factories, and the production capacity and decision-making power remain in American hands. Japan has long imagined that it is deepening its alliance and guaranteeing its own security, but in reality it is subsidizing America's manufacturing reshoring campaign. To be fair, the GlobalFoundries deal alone does not prove that Japan's semiconductor revival will fail. Japan has not abandoned its domestic semiconductor ambitions, with projects including its flagship chip-sector project Rapidus still moving forward. The Japanese government pledges to roll out subsidies to support local advanced process research and development. The crux of the problem, however, is whether Japan's fiscal situation can possibly bear the burden of both massive US-bound investment and its own domestic semiconductor revival at the same time. Japan's government debt-to-GDP ratio ranks the highest among all developed economies. The Takaichi government has ambitions to pour public-private investment totaling some $2.3 trillion through fiscal 2040 across 17 strategic Japanese sectors, including artificial intelligence and chips. The $550 billion investment commitment in the US is no small sum either. As more resources are funneled into American investment, how much is left for domestic plans becomes a real constraint. Investing in the US and reviving capabilities at home are not mutually exclusive, but whether Japan's finances can sustain both is an open question. Japan once sought to leverage the US-Japan alliance and draw on American supply chain resources to nurture its own domestic semiconductor capacity, with the ultimate aim of reviving its chip industry. But the GlobalFoundries project has laid bare the flaw in that thinking. The more Japan pours into the US, the more fragile its domestic semiconductor industry becomes, and the more its place in the global chip chain is locked into that of a supporting supplier to American industry. If Japan cannot wake up from the illusion that clinging to the US can revive its industry, the only outcome waiting for it is the wholesale hollowing out of its domestic semiconductor industry.

item.title: Ukraine's awkward position: Dependent on the US, powerless to push back
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 21:22:00
Ukraine Illustration: Liu Rui/GT Tension between the US and Ukraine has once again erupted into the open. Recent remarks by US Vice President JD Vance have laid bare a long-standing yet often obscured reality in US-Ukraine relations: Ukraine is not a formal US ally, and Washington does not want it to join NATO. Vance also called on Ukraine to stop striking Russian energy facilities. His comments appear to mark a clear boundary of US interests underpinning its Ukraine policy. The US may support Ukraine, but that does not mean it will underwrite every demand Kiev makes. Ukraine can rely on American aid, but it cannot expect Washington to stand unconditionally on its side. Vance has not articulated a brand-new policy. His statement is a public restatement of the current US administration's consistent position. The previous US administration, by contrast, stressed the moral imperative of supporting Ukraine, tying Ukrainian security closely to European security and US credibility, fostering a political relationship that resembled an alliance - despite the fact that Ukraine is not a NATO member, nor does it have a mutual defense treaty with the US. That it is not a formal ally has always been true. What stands out now is that the US no longer blurs this line deliberately, but proactively spells it out publicly. "Ukraine is trapped in an awkward, painful position. It cannot do without US assistance, yet it holds no leverage over Washington," Zhang Hong, a research fellow at the Institute of Russian, Eastern European and Central Asian Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times. Why is the US choosing this moment to publicly reaffirm this status? The answer lies in Vance's other demand: "Ukraine should stop attacking Russian energy facilities." An earlier diesel fuel deal struck between the US and Russia had already opened rifts in US-Ukraine relations. Compared with Ukraine's battlefield priorities, the US prioritizes its own energy market positioning and domestic political pressures. Compounding this, Washington has delayed deliveries of a batch of weapons to Ukraine. By partially cutting the aid pipeline while explicitly defining the bilateral relationship as non-allied, the US is essentially creating diplomatic cover to ratchet up pressure on Kiev. Should Ukraine's military actions run counter to core US interests, Washington can potentially scale back support and recalibrate its policy, laying full blame for escalation at Kiev's door. Aid is a discretionary favor, while rolling back support is seen as a legitimate policy choice - this has become the underlying logic of the US' Ukraine strategy. This does not mean Ukraine has lost its strategic value to the US. "In the European theater, the Ukraine crisis remains a key instrument for the US to sustain transatlantic security bonds. The US, in turn, retains sway over Europe's security agenda and reaps economic gains from defense industrial cooperation," Zhang explained. Toward Russia, the Ukraine crisis also serves as a vital topic for US diplomatic maneuvering. Whether negotiating ceasefire terms, security consultations or potential future energy and economic accords, Washington keeps the Ukraine crisis alive to preserve room for bargaining with Moscow, he added. Washington's support for Ukraine has never been an open-ended, unconditional moral obligation, but a strategic choice weighed rigorously against costs and benefits. Clearly, Ukraine's interests and grievances are never Washington's priority. Even when it comes to making the kind of deals Washington wants, Ukraine lacks the leverage to deliver. Ukraine's mineral resources available for potential deals are valued at around $500 billion, while potential joint projects between the US and Russia are worth as much as $14 trillion. By comparison, Ukraine's bargaining power is overwhelmingly outmatched. Ukraine has tried to tie itself to Europe, hoping European leaders would lobby Washington to sustain aid. Yet Europe maintains its own interest calculations, and the support it can offer Kiev is steadily dwindling. This leaves Ukraine stuck in a dilemma. The US is deliberately decoupling its own interests from Ukraine's aspirations. It has no objection to continuing to use the Ukraine issue to pressure Russia, yet refuses to assume treaty obligations for Ukraine's security goals. Partnership continues when Kiev's military moves align with Washington's objectives; when interests collide, Ukraine's demands are the ones usually sacrificed. From the moment Washington clarified the boundaries of US-Ukraine relations, one truth emerges: Ukraine has always been a geopolitical tool for the US, never its core interest. This unequal dynamic of dependence and limited bargaining power has left Ukraine in an awkward and passive position from the start.

item.title: China, Djibouti stress navigation freedom in Red Sea, urge restraint on force and unilateral sanctions amid Saudi-Houthi conflict
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 21:14:00
A crude oil tanker passes through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait as a Djibouti Coast Guard vessel conducts a surveillance patrol off Djibouti on September 29, 2026. Photo: VCG China and Djibouti have released a joint communique as Middle East tensions are spilling over into the Red Sea, imperiling regional security and trade. It underscores the importance of upholding freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and urges extra-regional powers to refrain from arbitrarily resorting to the use of force and unilateral sanctions so as to prevent further escalation of regional tensions. The joint communique, released by China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Thursday, followed a meeting in Beijing on Wednesday between Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, Djibouti's Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation. Djibouti, located in the Horn of Africa and separated from Yemen by the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, commands the critical waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, giving it great strategic significance. The joint statement notes that the recent escalation of tensions in the Red Sea poses a grave threat to the global economy. In particular, it endangers economic activities including trade, investment, energy and food security for countries in the Horn of Africa, and exacerbates security risks such as piracy and terrorism. The two sides hold that de-escalating tensions in the Middle East is key to addressing security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea. They call on all parties to take concrete actions through dialogue and diplomacy to tackle the severe challenges facing the Middle East, the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa, and prevent regional tensions from escalating or growing more complicated. The document further stresses the importance of upholding freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, stating that the navigation rights exercised by merchant vessels of all countries under international law should be respected. China supports Red Sea littoral states in safeguarding the safety and unimpeded flow of the international waterway and upholding shared regional interests in a constructive manner. According to Song Wei, a professor at the School of International Relations and Diplomacy at Beijing Foreign Studies University, the joint communique carries forward China's position articulated during UN Security Council deliberations on the Red Sea in July, with more systematic, clear elaboration. Unlike some prior statements centered merely on shipping safety, it places Red Sea security under the Horn of Africa's broader governance framework and addresses Middle East tensions, Red Sea shipping, refugee issues, piracy and food security as an integrated whole, Song added. The communique came as hostilities in Yemen reignited, with the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces locked in fierce clashes for control of the Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, renewing threats to the security of this critical international waterway. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said almost 260,000 people have been displaced since August. The persistent military escalation has drawn heightened diplomatic and security concern from regional and international powers. The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and family members to depart from its missions in Saudi Arabia, according to Reuters. French President Emmanuel Macron made a surprise visit to Riyadh Wednesday for talks on strategic ties and regional developments. On the same day, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El‑Sisi said Cairo would limit its defense commitments for Saudi Arabia to protecting Saudi territory and borders and would not involve attacking Yemen, according to media reports. In the joint communique, the two countries also call on the international community, especially external powers, to abandon double standards, respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of regional countries, and refrain from arbitrarily resorting to force and unilateral sanctions. "Unlike the practices of some external powers marked by military intervention, China and Djibouti adhere to a regional governance approach that puts regional countries in the driving seat and advances security and development in tandem," said Song. By aligning its position with China, Djibouti stands a better chance of winning broad recognition from Red Sea littoral states and countries across the Horn of Africa, said Song. "Amid mounting great‑power competition, the document advocates regional consultation to build consensus among littoral states. It rejects confrontational mindsets, guards against extra‑regional powers expanding military strength and stoking regional tensions in the name of safeguarding shipping‑lane safety, and keeps avenues open for diplomatic mediation," she noted. Notably, on issues concerning the Horn of Africa, the joint communique expresses firm support for Somalia in upholding its national sovereignty and territorial integrity. It rejects attempts to secure "diplomatic recognition" for Somaliland and opposes any form of collusion between Somaliland and Taiwan authorities. Prior to the release of the communique, during the talks between two countries' foreign minister on Wednesday, Wang Yi said that China appreciates Djibouti's adherence to the one-China principle. He also noted that China values the comprehensive strategic partnership between China and Djibouti and is willing to further deepen pragmatic cooperation with Djibouti, adding that both sides should give full play to China's zero-tariff policy and Djibouti's geographical advantages. The shared China‑Djibouti position on security and development also bears out the idea that sovereignty and territorial integrity are the cornerstone of a stable regional order, and connectivity plus economic and trade cooperation can provide a sustained, interest‑based underpinning for regional peace, Song noted.

item.title: Extended-stay travel gains ground among China's older people
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 13:21:00
This undated file photo shows elderly people practicing musical instruments at the Huangshan mutual aid community in Huangshan District of Huangshan City, east China's Anhui Province. (Xinhua) On a recent autumn morning in Xiongcun Village in east China's Anhui Province, Bi Sheng sipped coffee in his small studio while answering emails. A short walk away, craftsmen were renovating an old house, waiting for the 55-year-old to review designs and select timber. A native of Beijing, Bi first visited villages in Shexian County of Huangshan City, southern Anhui, more than a decade ago for a design project. Drawn to the area's rich cultural heritage, he eventually bought a house there and embraced what he described as a semi-retired life. "Every village has its own stories, and history is everywhere. That was beyond my expectations," he said. His new life has given Bi something he missed in the city: close-knit neighborhood ties. His new neighbors sometimes bring him freshly caught fish or vegetables they have grown themselves. "In cities, many people don't even know their neighbors," he said. Bi is part of a growing trend in China, where many older people are traveling to spend extended periods in places with beautiful scenery, rich culture and opportunities to build social connections, particularly after retirement. From July 2024 to June 2025, China recorded more than 84.3 million extended-stay visits by older travelers, averaging more than 7 million a month, according to a report released by the China Association of Ageing. To cash in on this fast-growing market, many regions offer services tailored to older travelers, ranging from age-friendly accommodations and traditional wellness treatments to activities that help newcomers build social connections. In Shexian County, at the foot of Mount Huangshan and within easy reach of major eastern cities such as Shanghai and Hangzhou, local authorities have developed eight wellness-themed guesthouses, said Xu Yuhong, deputy director of the county's health commission. These guesthouses received 13,300 guests from January to July this year, he said. Wu Zenghe is one of the guesthouse managers. He converted three traditional Huizhou-style buildings into a guesthouse catering to older travelers. "People who travel after retirement are more interested in in-depth experiences than in simply rushing from one tourist attraction to another," Wu said. His guesthouse features specially designed doors and windows to block noise and light, as well as herbal sachets intended to aid sleep. It also offers an artificial intelligence-powered health consultation device, acupuncture, moxibustion and medicinal baths. So far this year, it has welcomed several thousand older visitors from across China, including hundreds who stayed for more than a week. In Yunnan Province in southwest China, some markets have been renovated to better accommodate older people, while eligible visitors can receive discounts at tourist attractions and use public services such as universities for older adults. In Heilongjiang Province in northeast China, localities are exploring cross-border extended-stay and wellness initiatives for older visitors. At the same time, as older travelers spend weeks or months away from home, many want a stable social network and a sense of belonging. About 2,600 older people from across China live in the Huangshan mutual aid community in Huangshan District, Huangshan City. Li Jiankang, a 66-year-old from Nanjing, capital of neighboring Jiangsu Province, was among the community's first residents. His daily routine includes running, tending a vegetable garden, playing the saxophone, and joining other residents for table tennis or swimming. He said he has made many friends and found a fulfilling rhythm to life in Huangshan. The community has established more than 20 interest groups covering sports, agriculture and music, giving residents opportunities to connect through shared interests. It has also set up mutual aid groups so residents can care for one another. "Many older people who live alone can feel isolated, and some may even struggle with their mental health. That is why we hope to help them find comfort and companionship through mutual support," said Li Junping, manager of the community. "A sense of being needed is often the main reason residents choose to stay." For Li Jiankang, this sense of connection is central to the experience. "To me, the Chinese character for 'mutual' looks like two hands clasped together," he said. "Everyone here extends a hand to help others, and people can feel the bonds between us." Elderly women learn to make fish-shaped lanterns at a studio in Shexian County of Huangshan City, east China's Anhui Province, Jan. 30, 2026. (Photo by Shi Yalei/Xinhua)

item.title: EC president criticized for threatening China trade curbs despite hard-won talks
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 13:18:00
The European Union (EU) flags in front of EU headquarters in Brussels, Belgium. Photo: VCG European Commission (EC) President Ursula von der Leyen's renewed warnings of tougher trade restrictions against China, coming on the heels of hard-won bilateral agreements, have raised concerns that Brussels is resorting to threats and trade pressure that risk eroding bilateral trust, rather than addressing the structural problems holding back its own industries. The latest warnings follow intensive China-EU negotiations that yielded concrete gains for both sides, including progress in the automotive sector. Yet Brussels is considering further restrictions across additional industries, even as European businesses caution against the costs of protectionism. Chinese analysts said the EU's "talk-while-fighting" approach reflects its difficulties adjusting to a changing industrial landscape rather than newfound economic strength. They warned that threats and protectionism offer no remedy for Europe's internal challenges and could instead jeopardize recent agreements and erode the trust needed for future negotiations. Trade weapons, deeper troubles In a speech to the European Parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen said the bloc must be prepared to deploy "trade defense instruments" if dialogue fails to deliver results, even as she acknowledged progress in recent China-EU economic and trade consultations, according to a news release published on the EC's website. She called for swift safeguard measures when import surges threaten European industries. The Commission also plans to introduce a DiversifyEU package in December to reduce dependence on single suppliers, along with a new instrument to restrict access to the EU single market more quickly when its interests are threatened. The EU's tougher posture reflects its struggle to adapt to a changing industrial landscape, particularly as Chinese manufacturers have gained ground in electric vehicles and other emerging industries, Wang Yiwei, director of the Center for European Studies at Renmin University of China, told the Global Times on Thursday. Europe wants time to rebuild its industrial strength amid pressure from member states and domestic industries, hoping trade restrictions will provide temporary relief, Wang said. "But such measures cannot deliver the technological advances or industrial transformation needed for sustained growth." The challenge goes beyond individual products to the industrial systems and technologies shaping the future of manufacturing. Europe needs to strengthen its own capabilities rather than blame China for its internal shortcomings, Wang said. The EU's latest tough rhetoric follows a round of intensive China-EU trade talks in Beijing on October 8-9 , which produced 16 points of consensus across four areas, including an understanding on hybrid vehicle trade and further consultations on the EU's anti-subsidy case against Chinese electric vehicles, according to China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM). Von der Leyen on Wednesday credited EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic with progress in talks with China, citing greater predictability in rare-earth export controls and an understanding on Chinese-made hybrid vehicle exports. However, she argued that progress in one sector was insufficient to address broader trade imbalances, according to the EC's release. Analysts stressed that the hard-won outcomes of China-EU trade talks represent concrete, positive progress and tangible gains for both sides, particularly European businesses seeking greater certainty. Further EU trade restrictions could jeopardize those gains and call into question Brussels' own professed commitment to honoring agreements. The EU is stepping up efforts to introduce new trade defense tools, including proposals for a so-called "kill switch" to swiftly restrict market access and a European version of the US Section 301 mechanism. China has repeatedly criticized the proposed new tools as protectionist and unilateralist. Shi Xiaoli, director of the WTO Law Research Center at China University of Political Science and Law, told the Global Times that the EU's proposed measures are based on subjective assumptions rather than sufficient evidence, overlooking the fact that Chinese manufacturers' competitive advantages stem from innovation and a complete industrial supply chain that helps lower costs. She argued that such measures are discriminatory and arbitrary, raising questions about their compatibility with WTO rules. The price of protectionism Even as the EU takes a harder line on trade, there is also recognition of the risks of escalating tensions with China. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday backed stronger EU trade defense tools to address so-called unfair competition from China. But he said the bloc did not want to make use of its trade defense toolbox, stressing that the goal was to achieve a new balance in trade rather than trigger a conflict, according to Bloomberg. The economic costs of trade restrictions were highlighted by Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Källenius, who warned on the same day that protectionist measures could raise production costs and distort global supply chains. While greater restrictions could improve resilience, they would also make production more expensive, he said, warning that Europe shouldn't become "an island" cut off from major trading partners. European businesses have also urged caution over the broader use of trade restrictions. In a position paper released on Monday, BusinessEurope, a leading European business organization, said the EU should establish clear criteria to distinguish security-sensitive trade from ordinary commercial competition, emphasizing that not all trade with China carries the same risk. The group stressed that the EU must be transparent about where the costs of its trade measures would fall and be prepared to shoulder the responsibility, warning that China had signaled it would retaliate against EU actions. Wang said Europe's heavy reliance on global markets and supply chains makes trade restrictions particularly costly. "European manufacturers depend on Chinese intermediate goods, while German automakers also produce vehicles in China for export," he said. Responding to the EU's proposed "dual-track" approach, MOFCOM said both sides must demonstrate sincerity in resolving their differences through dialogue. It stressed that the EU should not expect to secure benefits through pressure or underestimate China's determination and ability to safeguard its own interests. Despite tensions, channels for China-EU engagement remain open. A delegation of 12 members of the European Parliament's Committee on International Trade will visit China from October 27 to 29 for talks with Chinese officials and lawmakers. Discussions are expected to cover market access, industrial subsidies, supply chains and critical raw materials, Euronews reported on Wednesday. Under the agreement reached in Beijing earlier this month, China and the EU are also scheduled to hold a ministerial-level video meeting in January 2027, followed by the third meeting of their Trade and Investment Consultation Mechanism in March. Shi urged the EU to take a more pragmatic approach to trade imbalances rather than invoke economic security concerns to pressure China. "Brussels should abandon confrontational thinking and seize opportunities arising from China's innovation-driven development to expand mutually beneficial cooperation in green development, new energy and digital industries," she said.

item.title: China-initiated Luban Workshops empower global youth with practical skills
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 08:09:00
Participants view exhibits at an exhibition during the World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference 2026 in Tianjin, north China, Oct. 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Ran) At an automotive industrial park in north China's Tianjin Municipality, Egyptian students Abdelrahman Ayman Zaky and Adham Ayman are gaining hands-on experience in new energy vehicle (NEV) chassis systems alongside their Chinese peers. Having acquired vocational skills at an Egyptian Luban Workshop, the two came to China to deepen their expertise. Adham, 20, hopes to improve his Chinese and vehicle maintenance skills before returning to Egypt to pursue a career as an automotive engineer. Their experience highlights the mission of the China-initiated Luban Workshops, which over the past decade have equipped young people worldwide with useful skills, fostered local talent, and supported industrial development. Named after Luban, an ancient Chinese craftsman and inventor who lived more than 2,500 years ago, the initiative draws on a longstanding Chinese tradition of craftsmanship and innovation. Jointly established by Chinese and foreign educational institutions, Luban Workshops now offer vocational education and skills-training programs in 32 countries. In Egypt, Luban Workshops are helping students like Adham translate classroom learning into engineering capabilities. Mohamed Mostafa, a student at an Egyptian Luban Workshop now studying at Tianjin Light Industry Vocational Technical College, said hands-on practice has strengthened his ability to tackle real-world engineering challenges. "In the EPIP (Engineering Practice and Innovation Project) classroom, we don't just work on simulated problems. We work on real-world engineering problems in teams, discussing solutions, refining our techniques and testing them again and again. We break down complex challenges to achieve the best results and meet engineering standards," Mostafa said. He added that he has shared the approach with students in Egypt, where they have applied the same methods to develop their own projects. The two Egyptian Luban Workshops have provided formal education to more than 3,100 people and skills training on over 4,000 occasions, creating new opportunities for industrial cooperation. Wang Baolong, dean of the School of Mechanical Engineering at Tianjin Light Industry Vocational Technical College, said graduates trained in advanced technologies can meet the needs of local businesses, strengthening Chinese companies' confidence in investing in and establishing factories in Egypt while supporting local economic development. An employment training base jointly established by the Egyptian Luban Workshops and the China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone has provided young Egyptians with a direct pathway to employment. "After receiving professional technical training, these young people can operate production equipment proficiently. They are exactly the kind of skilled workers that companies need," Wang added. Beyond teaching technical skills, the workshops also help build local capacity for sustained vocational training. While setting up training centers and supplying advanced equipment, Chinese partners send teachers and technicians to train local instructors and arrange exchanges and learning opportunities in China. In 2016, the Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College and the Ayutthaya Technical College in Thailand jointly established the world's first Luban Workshop. Over the past decade, all six of the workshop's internationalized majors have been incorporated into Thailand's national education system. "We are not just cultivating talent for the local area, but leaving the whole system behind. Chinese standards and models are truly integrating into and promoting local development," said Mei Wentao, a staff member at the Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College. More than 100 Chinese companies in Thailand operate businesses ranging from NEV components to vehicle distribution. In August 2025, the China-Thailand automotive intelligent manufacturing industry-education integration community was established in Thailand. With a steady supply of skilled graduates, companies can recruit directly from schools, helping young Thai people find jobs more easily and quickly. In Central Asia, the Tajik Luban Workshop is helping local young people explore new career opportunities. In nearly four years of operation, it has provided learning and training opportunities to more than 3,600 undergraduate and postgraduate students. When Bakhtiyor Bozorzoda enrolled at the Tajik Technical University, he was uncertain about his chosen major in geodesy and cartography. Advanced surveying equipment, digital mapping technologies, and virtual simulation courses at the Tajik Luban Workshop helped him recognize the field's potential and develop a stronger interest in surveying. During his studies, Bozorzoda gained hands-on experience with high-precision instruments and digital mapping technologies. "I hope to continue my studies in China in the future, learn more advanced surveying technologies and contribute to infrastructure development in Tajikistan," he said. Today, Luban Workshops have become a hallmark of China's international vocational education cooperation. Data from China's Ministry of Education show that the country has established 38 Luban Workshops in 32 countries, providing formal education to more than 30,000 students and non-degree training to over 160,000 people. The Luban Workshops reflect a commitment to harmony, coexistence and the common good in Chinese cultural tradition. By responding to local needs, they help young people in different countries acquire skills that can benefit them throughout their careers, said Tian Xuejun, president of the China Education Association for International Exchange, at the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, held in Tianjin from Oct. 15 to 17. China has the world's largest vocational education system, with 9,151 secondary vocational schools, 1,554 higher vocational colleges and 124 vocational undergraduate institutions. As of the end of 2025, China's vocational education catalog covered 19 major categories, 97 subcategories and 1,491 majors, spanning virtually all sectors of the national economy and all 41 major industrial categories. China is continuing to strengthen its vocational education system to support the development of emerging industries and expand opportunities for people both at home and abroad. At the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, representatives from 45 countries jointly released the Framework of World Vocational and Technical Education Standards developed under China's leadership. The framework calls for improving vocational school systems, establishing lifelong education and training opportunities for all, developing teaching materials through industry-education collaboration, building teaching teams through school-enterprise partnerships, and using artificial intelligence to drive reform in education and teaching.
